origin: Mountains and canyons of Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas, south through Mexico to Central America
habitat: Moist rocky canyons, seeps and springs in desert grassland, scrub and piñon–juniper–oak woodland, 3,900–6,600 ft
blurb: The red-flowered outlier of the lamb's-ear genus, and proof of how far Stachys ranges beyond silver foliage. Where lamb's ear is a woolly grey mat grown for leaves nobody looks at twice in bloom, scarlet hedgenettle is an upright, hairy, square-stemmed clump hung with narrow scarlet trumpets over a long season — and hummingbirds are its designated pollinators, taking the pollen on their foreheads as they feed. It is a Southwest canyon plant, not a Front Range native, and it wants what it gets at home: part shade and a moist, well-drained pocket rather than the bone-dry xeric bed its silver cousins prefer. Hardiness here is honestly marginal — worth growing for the hummingbirds, but plan on it being a short-lived perennial that may need replacing.
sun: Part shade to full sun — afternoon shade, east of a shrub or wall, is appreciated here
water: Moderate — NOT xeric; wants moist, well-drained soil and a deep soak every week or two through summer
spread: Upright, well-behaved clump — it does not run or take over
seasons: Fresh green, coarsely toothed foliage from late spring; scarlet tubular flowers in interrupted spikes from midsummer well into fall; dies back to the ground over winter
wildlife: A hummingbird plant first and foremost — hummingbirds are its designated pollinators, and its long bloom season overlaps both spring and fall migration; bees and butterflies work it too
toxic: No documented toxicity to people or pets, but no food use either — grow it as an ornamental
gaps: Reel covers spring, summer and fall from the plant's native Arizona/New Mexico range. No winter shot: it dies fully to the ground over winter here, so there is no winter presence to photograph — an honest skip, not a missing shot.

care.hardiness: Rated to USDA zone 6 and reported cold-hardy to about −20 °F, which on paper covers the Front Range (zones 5b–6a) — but be honest about it: growers on the semi-arid High Plains report it is not reliable about returning each winter, and recommend being prepared to replant.[3] Treat it as a short-lived or marginal perennial here rather than a permanent fixture. Its wild range sits at 3,900–6,600 ft in Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas, so the elevation is no obstacle; the cold winter wet and our hard freeze-thaw cycles are the real test.[2] Site it against a warm south or east wall, mulch the crown after the ground freezes, and give it perfect winter drainage to improve its odds.
care.planting: Plant out in late spring after the last frost, once the soil has genuinely warmed — mid-May on the Front Range — so it has a full season to build roots before its first winter.[4] Spring planting is much safer than fall for a zone-marginal plant like this one. In containers it is easy and blooms freely, but pot-grown roots are far less cold-hardy than the zone rating implies, so either sink the pot for winter or move it somewhere sheltered and barely moist.
care.sun: Part shade is what it takes in the wild, growing in moist canyon crevices and on shaded slopes.[1] Here it will take full sun if the soil stays moist, but it is happier with afternoon shade — planting it east of a shrub or wall so it gets morning sun and afternoon relief is the specific recommendation from growers in a comparable hot, dry, high-plains climate.[3]
care.soil: Moist but well-drained is the formula — it grows on rocky, sandy and riparian soils in the wild, and adapts readily to sand, loam or clay in the garden, including caliche and ordinary garden soil.[1][2][3] It handles our neutral-to-alkaline range, roughly pH 6.0–8.0.[1] The one thing it will not tolerate is a site that stays cold and waterlogged over winter; the drainage matters most in the dormant season.
care.water: Medium water — this is the plant in this guide's Stachys group that is genuinely not xeric, and treating it like lamb's ear will kill it.[1] Its wild habitat is moist canyons, seeps and springs, not dry slopes.[2] Roughly an inch of water every other week through the growing season suits it, more in a hot dry spell.[3] Mulch to hold soil moisture, and do not let it dry to wilting repeatedly.
care.spacing: Set plants 12–18 in apart; it makes an upright clump 1–1.5 ft across and does not run into its neighbours.[3] A loose group of three or five reads far better to a hummingbird than a single plant.
care.propagation: Grow it from seed — it is cultivated from seed and is commercially available, so seed is the straightforward route.[1] Sow in spring in warmth and grow the seedlings on to a good size before planting out, since a well-rooted plant has a much better chance of surviving its first Front Range winter. Softwood cuttings taken from non-flowering shoots in early summer root reasonably well, as with most mint-family plants, and are the way to hold on to a particular colour form (coral and brick-red selections exist alongside the wild scarlet).
care.bloom: In its native range it flowers from March through October, with the heaviest flush in early spring, carrying bright red tubular flowers ¾–1¼ in long in interrupted spikes of two to four.[1][2] On the Front Range the season shifts later — expect it to get going in midsummer once nights warm and to carry on until hard frost, which is exactly when late hummingbirds most need it. Deadheading spent spikes keeps new ones coming.
care.feeding: Light feeding at most. A single spring dressing of compost is plenty; heavy nitrogen produces lax growth that flops and enters winter soft, which is the last thing a marginally hardy plant needs.
care.maintenance: Deadhead spent flower spikes through the season to keep it blooming.[3] Leave the dead top growth standing over winter rather than cutting it back in fall — it traps snow and insulates the crown — and cut it to the ground in early spring as new shoots appear. Mulch the crown once the ground has frozen, and pull the mulch back in spring so the crown is not sitting damp.
care.troubles: The main risk is simply winter loss on a zone-marginal plant, which is a siting and drainage problem more than a disease problem.[3] Otherwise it is trouble-free: an aromatic mint-family plant with no serious pests, non-invasive in habit, and left alone by deer.[1][3] Do not let the 'nettle' in the name worry you — it does not sting; the name refers to the leaf shape.
care.companions: A hummingbird-garden plant, so pair it with the guide's other hummingbird nectar sources that share its moderate-water, part-shade-tolerant leanings — scarlet bugler penstemon, hummingbird mint, red hot poker and California fuchsia will keep birds working the same corner from early summer to frost. Keep it out of the xeric bed with the lamb's ears; it needs more water than they do.

edible.summary: Grown as a hummingbird ornamental — there is no documented food use for any part of it.[1][2]
edible.caution: Scarlet hedgenettle is not a food plant. No authority documents a culinary use for its leaves, flowers, roots or seeds, and it should not be eaten.[1][2] It is not known or listed to be poisonous either — it is an aromatic member of the mint family with no toxicity on record — but the absence of a poisoning report is not evidence of safety, and 'not documented as toxic' is a long way from 'edible'. Two name-based confusions are worth heading off: despite 'hedgenettle' it is not a nettle and does not sting, and despite 'Texas betony' it is not the European betony of herbal tradition (Betonica officinalis, long separated from Stachys), so do not substitute it in any preparation calling for betony.
